\title{One Timestamp Does Not Identify Temporal Support\\
in Event-Detection Benchmarks}
\author{Anonymous CVPR submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Event-detection benchmarks compare a prediction with a label at a single
nominal timestamp, and that timestamp does not identify when the evidence
supporting the prediction was acquired or which instant its output represents.
This paper measures two predictor-side quantities and establishes a complementary
limit on attributing within-exposure event timing to object timing using released
artifacts. For a released
recurrent detector, the newest \rvtWindow\,ms input window has an
occlusion-sensitivity centroid \rvtCentroidMagMeas\,ms before the label instant,
while the regression-based temporal coefficient estimated on nominal-time-matched
detections with centered label velocity is
$\ladderFullTau\,\pm\,\ladderFullTauSE$\,ms, statistically consistent with zero
under the reported specification. Across the evaluated specifications with
geometric controls, the coefficient ranges from \satLo{} to \satHi{} ms, whereas
the newest-window occlusion-sensitivity centroid corresponds to
$+\rvtCentroidMagMeas$ ms under the convention of Eq.~2. On the velocity-evaluable subset,
average precision is nearly invariant
between the label instant and the newest-window occlusion-sensitivity centroid:
applying the corresponding center displacement changes mAP by only
\mapCostAbs{} absolute mAP (\mapCost{} percentage points, \mapCostPct\,\%
relative to \mapZero{}) and reorders none of the \rankCkpts{} checkpoints at the
measured centroid displacement.
On the label side,
DSEC's ceiling-exposure sequences carry a harmonic signature at
\flickerLineHz\,Hz, showing that within-exposure event timing cannot be
attributed to object timing without separating illumination structure.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

An object detection benchmark evaluates a prediction $\hat{s}$ against a ground
truth $s^{*}$ through a function $\rho(\hat{s},s^{*})$ of position, shape and
class, indexed by a query time $t$. The query time selects which label the
prediction is compared against. Beyond selecting the label at query time $t$, the
scoring function contains no variable representing temporal support or effective state
time, so a temporal discrepancy is scored as displacement. Neither side's
temporal support is specified by that nominal instant. A predictor computes $\hat{s}$ from a
window of sensor data. A label is produced by an exposure, an annotator or
tracker working on the exposed image, and a geometric transfer into another
sensor's frame.

The released input-window convention is fixed by the detector configuration and is
measurable from released artifacts. The detector's full recurrent temporal support is
not identified by that convention. The event branch of the detector examined
here~\cite{gehrig2023rvt} consumes a window of \rvtWindow\,ms divided into
\rvtBins{} bins, and the preprocessing script of its own repository builds the
window boundaries by counting backwards from label timestamps, so each window
ends at the label it is scored against (Sec.~\ref{sec:window}). Under uniform
weighting the evidence in such a window is centered \rvtCentroidMag\,ms before
the instant the label asserts. Whether the trained network's bin sensitivities
are uniform is a separate question, and occluding each bin in turn on real
validation samples answers it: the occlusion-sensitivity centroid is
\rvtCentroidMeas\,ms (Sec.~\ref{sec:influence}). This defines a measured
center-displacement interval between the newest-window sensitivity centroid and
the label instant. It does not identify the centroid of the detector's full
recurrent support.

The training target is indexed at the label instant, and the
measurement of Sec.~\ref{sec:outputtime} is consistent with it, at
\ladderFullTau\,$\pm$\,\ladderFullTauSE\,ms, which is a failure to reject and not
a demonstration that they coincide. The objective does not require the
regression-based coefficient to equal the newest-window occlusion-sensitivity centroid.
Under the reported specification, their point estimates differ by \outInterval\,ms.
The velocity that measurement regresses on is finite differenced from the same
labels the residual is measured against, and a forward difference shares their
noise, returning an offset from a detector that has none. The estimator is therefore calibrated on synthetic tracks before it is used,
and carries a placebo term on which no lag can load.

The second measurement concerns the same class of undeclared timing property on
the label side. DSEC
publishes each frame's own exposure interval, and across the \dsecSeqCount{}
training sequences whose exposure files resolve, the width varies by a factor of
\dsecExpRatio{} against a frame period fixed at \dsecFramePeriod\,ms, with
\dsecPinnedFrac\,\% of frames pinned at an auto-exposure ceiling of
\dsecExpMax\,\micro s in \dsecCeilingSeqs{} sequences (Fig.~\ref{fig:exposure}).
Those \dsecCeilingSeqs{} carry the harmonic series of a \flickerLineHz\,Hz mains
flicker, and between
\sixLockedLoPct\,\% and \sixLockedHiPct\,\% of labeled boxes carry more power at
the fundamental than at an off-frequency arm on the same events
(Sec.~\ref{sec:flicker}). A \flickerPeriodUs\,\micro s illumination period within a
\dsecExpMax\,\micro s exposure induces temporal structure in the event stream
without object motion, and
Sec.~\ref{sec:cost} reports what that leaves of a per-object statistic.

The single timestamp used by the metric does not specify the temporal support of
either side of the comparison. We measure two predictor-side quantities and
establish a complementary limit on attributing within-exposure event timing to
object timing. The first is the
occlusion-sensitivity profile of a released recurrent event detector. Its newest
window has an occlusion-sensitivity centroid \rvtCentroidMagMeas\,ms before the
label instant and accounts for \histShareTwenty\,\% of the summed window-ablation
sensitivity measured over a \histHorizonB\,ms horizon. The second is the
regression-based temporal coefficient of the same checkpoint, estimated on
nominal-time-matched detections under Eq.~2. It is estimated
with a vector regression, a placebo term, and a sign-flip control on the velocity
estimator. The estimate is consistent with the label instant and is
\outInterval\,ms from the newest-window centroid. DSEC provides a complementary
exposure-side attribution case study: a harmonic series at \flickerLineHz\,Hz in
\dsecCeilingSeqs{} ceiling-exposure sequences shows that a within-box temporal
statistic measured inside one published exposure window cannot, by itself, be
attributed to object timing (Secs.~\ref{sec:window}--\ref{sec:flicker}).

The predictor- and label-side analyses are complementary case studies on separate
released benchmarks. They do not jointly decompose one detector--label pair.

The primary claim concerns identifiability under the metric. Displacing the
ground truth across the measured interval moves mAP by \mapCost{} points and
reorders none of the \rankCkpts{} released checkpoints. A common displacement
sweep also reveals a localized inversion between \texttt{rvt-b} and S5-S in the
$25$--$50$\,px/s stratum. The same interval is \outPxNinety\,px of displacement at the
ninetieth percentile of label speed and \outPxNinetynine\,px at the
ninety-ninth, Tab.~\ref{tab:strata} locates the insensitivity in the speed
composition of the benchmark rather than in an absence of displacement.

We measure input-side temporal sensitivity in released event detectors. We further
estimate a regression-based temporal coefficient under the reported
specification and compare it with the newest-window sensitivity centroid. On the
velocity-evaluable subset, standard average precision changes little over the
label-to-centroid displacement. A separate DSEC case study limits attribution of
within-exposure event timing to object timing.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Recovering a time offset from image-plane displacement.} Qin and
Shen~\cite{qin2018temporal} model a global camera--IMU time offset by shifting
feature observations with image-plane velocity and jointly optimizing the offset
with visual--inertial states and feature locations. Here the offset lies between
a predictor's clock and
a \emph{benchmark's} label clock. Streaming perception~\cite{li2020streaming}
folds wall-clock compute latency into average precision and re-anchors any
detector from box coordinates alone, later work adapts to the measured runtime
delay~\cite{yang2022streamyolo}, a continuous-stream framework scores the latest
available output against high-rate ground truth and reports reordered
rankings~\cite{chu2026stare}, and temporal tolerance has been argued for
time-series event detection~\cite{softed2024}. Each of those latencies is the
time from an event to an output and falls as the device gets faster. Sensor
latency, the illumination-dependent delay between a change and the timestamp the
sensor assigns it, is measured at
microseconds~\cite{yang2024latency}, and nighttime event imaging corrects an
illumination-dependent trailing by learning a per-event timestamp
calibration~\cite{liu2024nighttime}, both target the sensor, while here the
released exposure metadata and event stream bound what a within-box temporal
statistic computed inside one published exposure can be attributed to. Inside
the citation graph of LET-3D-AP~\cite{hung2022let}, a latency-aware average
precision scores 3D detection at the instant a prediction becomes available on
a named device~\cite{rethink3d2025}. That work addresses compute latency,
whereas the interval measured in Sec.~\ref{sec:extrapolation} is fixed by a data representation. The
event--RGB frequency mismatch is named in~\cite{faod2024}, which scores with
unmodified average precision.

Mao et al.~\cite{mao2019delay} showed that video-detection AP can remain stable
despite temporal detection delay and introduced Average Delay to expose that
effect. This work examines which acquisition and label times are represented by
a nominal benchmark timestamp. We measure predictor-side sensitivity and constrain
within-exposure event-timing attribution using released detector and exposure
artifacts.

\paragraph{Decomposing localization error along a privileged axis.}
LET-3D-AP~\cite{hung2022let} decomposes camera-only 3D localization error along
the line of sight and defines an average precision tolerant of the longitudinal
part, and reports a camera-to-label synchronization gap as a per-dataset interval
that depends on horizontal object position. Sec.~\ref{sec:outputtime} keeps the
idea of a privileged axis but replaces the sensor's line of sight with the
object's own velocity vector, and estimates a time rather than defining a
tolerant score.
TIDE~\cite{bolya2020tide,hoiem2012diagnosing} and DETAD~\cite{alwassel2018detad}
bucket detection error atemporally, so a temporal offset falls inside their
localization bucket, and HOTA~\cite{luiten2021hota} takes the label clock as
exact.

\paragraph{Per-object time in labels.} Waymo's \texttt{camera\_synced\_box} solves
$t_{\mathrm{capture}}$ per object and stores the resulting box shift rather than
the time~\cite{waymolabelproto,sun2020waymo}. Miro et
al.~\cite{nunez2026annotations} measure within-frame per-object annotation
offsets on Argoverse\,2 and TruckScenes and define a dispersion of the
\emph{spatial} error. Each computes a per-object time in order to remove it. The
event-vision label formats carry the field: the Prophesee dtype used by Gen1, the
1\,Mpx dataset and DSEC-Det has a per-box \texttt{t}. In the releases examined
here, that field's per-object degree of freedom is not specified. Across the \ddSeqs{} released DSEC-Det
sequences, \ddBoxes{} boxes take \ddDistinctT{} distinct values of \texttt{t},
\ddBoxesPerT{} boxes per value, and those values are the \dsecFramePeriod\,ms
frame clock.

\paragraph{Event benchmarks and their exposures.}
Gen1~\cite{detournemire2020gen1} labels are drawn on gray-level images assembled
from asynchronous per-pixel measurements. On the 1\,Mpx
dataset~\cite{perot2020megapixel} the event count inside a labeled box at its own
timestamp is often too small to support detection~\cite{kugele2023howmany}.
DSEC-Det~\cite{gehrig2024lowlatency} labels by tracking~\cite{pang2021qdtrack} on
rectified frames and warps into the event view, and
Ev-3DOD~\cite{cho2025ev3dod} interpolates lower-rate annotations into high-rate
3D labels. That a frame's exposure is long relative to event timing has been
stated: Event-based deblurring~\cite{sun2023refid} argues that accumulating events from a single
frame timestamp loses information, deblurring work names auto-exposure as why the
width is unknown~\cite{kim2022unknownexposure}, and RENet~\cite{zhou2022renet}
uses a DSEC exposure interval as its event window while describing it as short.
The cited works do not read the released per-frame widths or measure what is
inside one. State space backbones~\cite{zubic2024ssm} substantially reduce sensitivity to
inference-time window duration, and
adaptive spatial-temporal windows~\cite{sui2026astw} retrain a detector under
each of nine partitioning strategies and report the score of each. Both treat the
window as a design variable to choose. Here, the released window configuration is
treated as a measured property of the released detector and evaluation pipeline.
That the released window is causal is already in print:
LEOD~\cite{wu2024leod} states that event detectors take only events triggered
before the query time, and builds a time-flip augmentation on the consequence
that forward inference favors receding objects. It does not measure where inside
that window the evidence sits. Protocol
work supplies the standards these measurements are held
to~\cite{oncalibration2024,stratification2024,northcutt2021labelerrors,ercan2023evreal}:
a repaired protocol can reverse a field's conclusion, and a reported score is
an estimate with a variance. A protocol audit can expose failures in what a
benchmark identifies even when the resulting correction reorders no existing
method. Average precision is nearly invariant over the label-to-centroid interval,
while the regression places the coefficient away from the occlusion-sensitivity
centroid under the reported specification.

\section{Comparison of input sensitivity and regression-based output timing}
\label{sec:predictor}

\subsection{Definition}

Let a predictor $P$ emit a state at query time $t$. A signed effective-weight
model uses bin centers $c_k$ and weights $a_k$ with $\sum_k a_k=1$, giving the
effective timestamp offset $\tau_P=\sum_k a_kc_k$ under constant velocity. The
empirical ablation profile instead assigns non-negative sensitivities $s_k\geq0$
to bins and has centroid $c_s=\sum_k s_kc_k/\sum_k s_k$. These are distinct
quantities: zero-ablation sensitivity depends on both the predictor and the
input, and is not in general a decomposition of temporal weights. Sections~\ref{sec:window}--\ref{sec:influence} measure this
operational input-sensitivity profile over the newest window. Section~\ref{sec:outputtime}
estimates the regression coefficient $\tau$ under Eq.~2. Interpreting $-\tau$ as an
effective state-time offset requires the absence of residual velocity-proportional
spatial bias.
Section~\ref{sec:extrapolation} compares $-c_s$ with the regression coefficient
$\tau$, equivalently $c_s$ with the effective timestamp $\tau_P=-\tau$.

\subsection{The window and the instant it is indexed by}
\label{sec:window}

Two released files fix the input side. The dataset configuration
\texttt{config/dataset/gen1.yaml} of the detector's own
repository~\cite{gehrig2023rvt} names the representation
\texttt{stacked\_histogram\_dt=50\_nbins=10}, a window of \rvtWindow\,ms divided
into \rvtBins{} bins of \rvtBinWidth\,ms. Line \rvtSourceLine{} of
\texttt{scripts/genx/preprocess\_dataset.py} constructs the array
\texttt{ev\_repr\_timestamps\_us\_end} by counting backwards from a label
timestamp in steps of the window duration, and extends it between consecutive
label timestamps. Each representation is therefore indexed by the end of its
window, and those ends are placed on label times. A window attached to a label at
time $t$ holds the events of $[t-\rvtWindow\,\mathrm{ms},\,t]$, whose uniform
weighting centroid falls \rvtCentroidMag\,ms before the instant $t$ at which the
label asserts a state. Both statements are read from the released source, and
the \rvtCentroidMag\,ms figure is a reference point rather than a property of
the trained network.

\subsection{The measured influence profile}
\label{sec:influence}

The newest-window occlusion-sensitivity centroid is computed from the measured
bin-ablation sensitivities of a released checkpoint. We take \rvtInfluenceSamples{} samples of the released Gen1
validation split with the released \texttt{rvt-t} checkpoint, warm the recurrent
state for \rvtWarmSteps{} steps, and occlude each bin in turn. For sample $i$, let
$Y_i$ denote the emitted detection tensor from the unoccluded input and
$Y_i^{(-k)}$ the tensor obtained after zeroing temporal bin $k$ while keeping the
incoming recurrent state identical. We define the influence of bin $k$ as
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
s_k&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\frac{\left\|Y_i^{(-k)}-Y_i\right\|_2}{\left\|Y_i\right\|_2},\quad N=480,\\
c_s&=\frac{\sum_k s_k c_k}{\sum_k s_k},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $c_k$ is the center time of bin $k$ relative to the label instant. The
occluded forward pass receives the same incoming recurrent state as the
corresponding reference pass, and its returned state is discarded. The profile is
a property of the current window and not of a perturbed history.

The profile is balanced between the two halves of the window (Fig.~\ref{fig:predictor}a)
and yields an occlusion-sensitivity centroid of \rvtCentroidMeas\,ms, compared
with \rvtCentroidUnif\,ms for uniform weighting. The released configuration
therefore places the measured centroid near the window reference without implying
uniform network sensitivity.
This is the current window's occlusion-sensitivity profile with the recurrent
state held fixed, not a decomposition of the full temporal support.

\paragraph{Recurrent support beyond the newest window.}
The detector is recurrent, so its temporal support does not end at the newest window. Occluding
past windows and propagating their state to the current step shows that the
newest accounts for \histShareTwenty\,\% of the summed window-ablation sensitivity
over a \histHorizonB\,ms horizon.
The tail does not decay to zero within that second, so
the window-ablation-sensitivity centroid follows the horizon instead of converging:
\histCentroidTen\,ms over \histHorizonA\,ms of history and
\histCentroidTwenty\,ms over \histHorizonB\,ms. The full recurrent temporal
support is not identified by this sensitivity measurement.

\paragraph{Across the released checkpoints and a second architecture.}
RVT releases three Gen1 checkpoints differing only in embedding width, attention
head dimension and FPN depth. SSM-ViT~\cite{zubic2024ssm} releases two more in
which each stage's ConvLSTM is replaced by an S5 state space layer, at \ssmParamsS{}
and \ssmParamsB{} M parameters against RVT's \capParamsS{} and \capParamsB{}.
It distributes RVT's own preprocessed Gen1 and inherits its window construction. On the same sequences, and
driving each the way its own release drives it, all \archCkpts{} checkpoints put the
newest window's occlusion-sensitivity centroid between \archHi{} and \archLo\,ms, none further than
\archUnifMax\,ms, or \archUnifPct\,\% of one bin, from the uniform-weight value.
The state the SSM release carries between evaluation chunks reaches none of its
outputs. Under the released streaming evaluation, this bounds the available
recurrent history to at most the current \ssmEvalChunk{}-window chunk. It ranges
from one to \ssmEvalChunk{} windows with position in the chunk, as the supplement
measures. The support behind that
window is not fixed in the same way either: over \capSamples{} samples of the
three RVT capacities, the newest window's share of a \capHorizon\,ms horizon
falls from \capShareT\,\% to \capShareB\,\% and the sensitivity centroid moves
from \capSuppT{} to \capSuppB\,ms.

\subsection{Regression-based temporal coefficient}
\label{sec:outputtime}

The influence profile is a statement about the network's input. Even a predictor
with uniform local sensitivity can emit a state describing a later instant,
and that quantity is measured from the same checkpoint's own detections.

A detector reporting the state an object occupied $\tau$ earlier incurs the
physical displacement $-\tau v$, where $v$ is the latent true velocity. We
observe only the finite-differenced label velocity $\tilde v=v+\eta$ and
therefore fit Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg} using $\tilde v$. Thus
$\tau=-\tau_{P}$ on the axis of Sec.~\ref{sec:predictor}. With $\hat{c}$ the
predicted center, $c^{*}$ the label center, $A$ the area of the ground-truth
box, $\hat{u}=\tilde v/\lVert \tilde v\rVert$ and $\mathrm{R}$ a quarter turn,
$b$ is a two-dimensional intercept, fitted globally or as per-sequence
intercepts in the reported specification,

\begin{equation}
\hat{c}-c^{*}=b-\tau\,\tilde v+\rho\,\mathrm{R}\tilde v+\gamma\sqrt{A}\,\hat{u}+\varepsilon
\label{eq:outreg}
\end{equation}

\noindent is fitted by stacking both components of every match into one least
squares problem, with standard errors clustered by sequence. It is the temporal
calibration of~\cite{qin2018temporal} carried to a box center, taken as a slope
rather than as the per-object ratio $-\langle
\hat{c}-c^{*},\hat{u}\rangle/\lVert \tilde v\rVert$, whose variance diverges as its
denominator approaches zero. For comparison, the per-object ratio evaluated on
the same rows has a mean of
$\ratioMean\,\pm\,\ratioMeanSE$\,ms, on the hypothesis evaluated in
Sec.~\ref{sec:extrapolation}, with an interquartile range of \ratioIQR\,ms.
Written this way the
regression estimates a regression-based temporal coefficient under
Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg}: no magnitude of the residual is taken, and $\tau$
does not load on a direction estimated from the same noisy velocity.
The reported full specification adds four coordinate/size regressors and
per-sequence intercepts to the terms displayed in Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg}.
The coefficient is a temporal offset only if no velocity-proportional spatial
bias remains after these controls. Such a bias is indistinguishable from $\tau$ in Eq.~2.

$\mathrm{R}\tilde v$ is the label velocity rotated a quarter turn. Because a pure
temporal offset acts along $\tilde v$ rather than $\mathrm{R}\tilde v$, $\rho$ serves
as a negative-control coefficient. A nonzero value indicates residual spatial
misspecification.
$\sqrt{A}\,\hat{u}$ absorbs a displacement along travel proportional to box side,
which is needed because that residual grows with box size and box size correlates
with label speed at \outSpeedSizeCorr{} on this split.

\paragraph{The finite difference used for the velocity.}
$\tilde v$ is finite differenced from labels, and the choice of difference changes
the answer. A forward difference $(c^{*}_{k+1}-c^{*}_{k})/\Delta$ carries the
label noise $\delta_{k}$ of the current center with weight $-1/\Delta$, and the
residual $\hat{c}-c^{*}_{k}$ carries the same $\delta_{k}$ with weight $-1$,
so their covariance is $\operatorname{Var}(\delta)/\Delta$ when $\tau$ is exactly
zero. A backward difference carries $\delta_{k}$ with the opposite sign and
produces the opposite artifact. The centered difference
$(c^{*}_{k+1}-c^{*}_{k-1})/(\Delta_{f}+\Delta_{b})$ does not use $c^{*}_{k}$ and
removes the direct same-frame shared-noise term. Residual bias from temporally
correlated annotation errors is not identified by this construction. Fitting all three is therefore a control on the estimator
itself, calibrated before use. On \synTracks{} synthetic tracks whose detector
has no lag whatever, with label centers corrupted at the dispersion the
supplement's difference ladder measures on Gen1 (\labelSigmaGen\,px), the forward
estimator returns \synFwd\,ms and the backward one \synBack\,ms against a closed
form of \synPred\,ms, they sum to \synSum\,ms, and removing the label noise
returns all three to \synZero\,ms. The same simulation recovers an injected lag
at \synRecover{} of its size, the attenuation an errors-in-variables treatment
predicts at \synLambda{} for this noise.

\paragraph{Regression dataset and matching.}
The released checkpoint is run over the Gen1 validation split with its recurrent
state carried across steps, and its detections at each labeled frame are matched
to the ground truth at an overlap of \outIoUfloor{} or above. The estimate is
conditional on detections matched at the nominal label time and applies only to
matches satisfying this association criterion.
Requiring both
label neighbors, so that a centered velocity exists, and discarding the matches
whose two neighbors coincide on the integer label lattice, leaves \outMatches{}
of \outRowsTotal{} over \outSeqs{} sequences at a median overlap of \outIoUmedian{}. Gen1's \texttt{track\_id} is a per-frame index rather
than a persistent identifier, so association is rebuilt independently between
adjacent label times. For each source box, candidate boxes of the same class are
scored by IoU, the highest-scoring candidate is selected, and the link is retained
only when IoU is at least \outIoUfloor{}. Ties follow the stored box order. This
greedy rule does not enforce global one-to-one matching or carry identities across
more than one interval. No speed floor is imposed.
Accordingly, this coefficient characterizes the subset of detections that can be
associated with ground truth at the nominal label time under the stated matching
rule. It is not an unconditional timing estimate over all detector outputs.

Table~\ref{tab:outtime} is a specification ladder, and the specification was
chosen by the placebo rather than by $\tau$. Under Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg} with only
the box-side term, $\tau=\ladderMinTau\,\pm\,\ladderMinTauSE$\,ms, but $\rho$ is
\ladderMinPl\,ms at \ladderMinPlSigmas{} standard errors, which indicates a term
omitted from Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg} that $\mathrm{R}\tilde v$ is a proxy for. A split by
the sign of the horizontal velocity locates it: $\rho$ changes sign across that
split, at \plRight\,ms and \plLeft\,ms, which a rotational term would not do.
Most label motion here is horizontal, so $\mathrm{R}\tilde v$ maps a horizontal speed
onto a vertical residual. A bias differing between oncoming and same-direction
traffic is represented by this rotated regressor. Entering
box height and image row along $\hat{y}$ and box width and image column along
$\hat{x}$, and then a constant vector per sequence, returns the placebo to
\ladderFullPl\,ms at \ladderFullPlSigmas{} standard errors. That is the
specification reported, and the criterion that selected it is a coefficient on a
regressor orthogonal to $\tilde v$.

Conditional on the reported specification, the regression-based temporal coefficient is
$\tau=\ladderFullTau\,\pm\,\ladderFullTauSE$\,ms. Across the evaluated
geometric-control specifications, $\tau$ ranges from \satLo{} to \satHi{} ms,
whereas the occlusion-sensitivity centroid corresponds to
$+\rvtCentroidMagMeas$ ms under the convention of Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg}. A
cluster bootstrap over sequences puts the \bootCI\,\% interval at
[\outBootLo,\,\outBootHi]\,ms. Under the full control set, a perturbation injected directly along
the fitted temporal regressor is recovered at \injRecovery{} of its magnitude.
The reported standard error and bootstrap interval condition on the selected
specification and omit specification-selection uncertainty.
Including all four geometric terms on both axes gives
$\satTau\,\pm\,\satTauSE$\,ms.

\subsection{Separation between input sensitivity and regression-based temporal coefficient}
\label{sec:extrapolation}

The comparison combines measurements under different recurrent-state conditions.
The centroid uses an eight-step warm-up with the incoming state fixed during
ablation. The regression uses detections from the validation stream with the
released state carried across frames. These are operational timing measurements
of the same checkpoint, not estimates of a common full-recurrent-support
centroid. Under the reported specification and its
annotation-error assumptions, the point-estimate difference is \outInterval\,ms. The regression
coefficient has a standard error of \outIntervalSE\,ms. This is a regression-coefficient
result rather than a latency estimate of this architecture. On the
convention of Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg} the centroid
hypothesis is $\tau=+\rvtCentroidMagMeas$\,ms, and no specification carrying
geometric controls reaches it: $\tau$ spans \satLo{} to \satHi\,ms across them.
Thus, \rvtCentroidMagMeas\,ms is the measured separation between the label
instant and the newest-window occlusion-sensitivity centroid, whereas \outInterval\,ms
is the point-estimate difference between that centroid and the reported regression
coefficient. The centroid of the full
recurrent support is not identified within the measured horizon. The standard
error quoted is the output-time term's. The variation across specifications is substantial
relative to the reported standard error and is not captured by that standard error.

The detector is trained against the ground truth at the label time on a window
ending there, so a measured offset near zero is consistent with the training
objective indexed at the label time. The objective
does not enforce the
interval, and the instant the output describes and the centroid of the evidence
used to produce it are different quantities that one benchmark timestamp stands
for. At the ninetieth percentile of label speed on this split, \outSpeedNinety\,px/s, the
\rvtCentroidMagMeas\,ms is \outPxNinety\,px of displacement, comparable to the
annotation dispersion of the labels themselves (\labelSigmaGenAnn\,px), and at the
ninety-ninth it is \outPxNinetynine\,px. That occlusion-sensitivity centroid and
the regression-based temporal coefficient are measurable from released artifacts alone.

\centering
\figasset{figs/fig6_sweep_real.pdf}{0.95\columnwidth}
\caption{One validation frame of the sweep of Fig.~\ref{fig:predictor}b:

above 20\,px/s, its fastest label moves \sweepRealFast\,px/s, so the two

\label{fig:sweepreal}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Effect on benchmark mAP.}
The benchmark metric can be evaluated in its own units: we translate each ground-truth box
center by $\delta\tilde v$, keeping its size and class fixed. This provides a
first-order surrogate for temporal displacement under local constant velocity.
The released predictions remain untouched. A detection
carries no velocity of its own. Over \mapFrames{} frames and \mapGT{} boxes,
\mapGTvelPct\,\% of which carry a centered velocity and the rest are ignored. Ground-truth
boxes without a centered velocity are marked ignored during evaluation, and detections
matched to ignored boxes are excluded from TP/FP accounting. The resulting mAP against
$\delta$ is smooth with its maximum at \mapArgmax\,ms
(Fig.~\ref{fig:predictor}b). On the axis of Eq.~\ref{eq:outreg} that is
$\tau=\mapArgmaxTau$\,ms, and mAP varies by at most \mapCost{} points over the
interval. This descriptive curve does not by itself identify a preferred temporal
value.

The full $-60$ to $+60$\,ms sweep moves mAP by \mapSweepSpan{} points. On the
$-50$ to $+30$\,ms grid summarized in Table~\ref{tab:strata}, the all-moving
span is \stSpanAll{} points. Displacing the ground truth to the window's centroid
costs \mapCostAbs{} absolute mAP (\mapCost{} percentage points,
\mapCostPct\,\% relative to \mapZero{}). On the velocity-evaluable subset, standard
average precision is nearly invariant over
the measured label-to-centroid displacement. At the
common $-\rvtCentroidMagMeas$\,ms displacement, the ordering of all
\rankCkpts{} released checkpoints is unchanged. Separately, scoring each
checkpoint at its own preferred displacement leaves the reported ordering
unchanged in the reported strata. A common displacement sweep reveals one localized
inversion between \texttt{rvt-b} and S5-S in the 25--50\,px/s stratum.
Table~\ref{tab:strata} locates the
flatness in that composition: \stShareSlow\,\% of the moving boxes travel below
\mapCutLo\,px/s, where the displacement is \stPxSlow\,px, and the sweep deepens
to \mapSpanHigh{} points between \mapCutMid{} and \mapCutHi\,px/s, where it is
\stPxHigh\,px, past the labels' own annotation dispersion of
\labelSigmaGenAnn\,px (Supplement Sec.~3). The pooled response is
composition-dependent: the mAP span is \stSpanAll{} points over all moving
boxes but increases to \mapSpanHigh{} points in the
\mapCutMid--\mapCutHi{}\,px/s stratum, where the centroid displacement costs
\stCostHigh{} points.

\section{A complementary within-exposure attribution limit}
\label{sec:flicker}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\figasset{figs/fig1_dsec_exposure.pdf}{0.95\textwidth}
\caption{Published per-frame exposure width across the \dsecSeqCount{} DSEC
training sequences whose exposure files resolve: per sequence (left, log axis,
median, interquartile range and \pctBandLo--\pctBandHi\,\% band, against the
fixed \dsecFramePeriod\,ms frame period) and pooled over \dsecFrameCount{}
frames (right). \dsecPinnedFrac\,\% of frames sit at the auto-exposure ceiling
of \dsecExpMax\,\micro s and \dsecExpGapCount{} fall between the largest
non-ceiling width of \dsecExpGapLo\,\micro s and that ceiling. This creates a
separated ceiling-versus-non-ceiling exposure regime. The \dsecCeilingSeqs{} ceiling sequences are
the ones measured in Sec.~\ref{sec:flicker}.}
\label{fig:exposure}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Exposure and labels}
\label{sec:labelclock}

The predictor-side analysis concerns the temporal support of released detector
inputs and outputs. DSEC provides a separate exposure-side analysis: published
exposure intervals bound the interval within which event timing is observed, while
illumination structure can introduce temporal variation unrelated to object motion.
DSEC~\cite{gehrig2021dsec} publishes
per-frame exposure metadata, and the files resolve
for
\dsecSeqCount{} train sequences. The width varies by a factor of
\dsecExpRatio{} against a frame period fixed at \dsecFramePeriod\,ms, and within
one recording by up to a factor of \dsecWithinSeqRatio{}. The auto-exposure
ceiling of \dsecExpMax\,\micro s holds \dsecPinnedFrac\,\% of frames, in
\dsecCeilingSeqs{} of the \dsecSeqCount{} sequences, and the distribution is not
continuous over that range (Fig.~\ref{fig:exposure}). This motivates treating
ceiling exposure as a distinct stratum.

The released DSEC-Det labels comprise \ddBoxes{} boxes on \ddTracks{} tracks
across \ddSeqs{} sequences, every label sits on the frame clock, and the median
spacing between consecutive label times is \ddSpacingMedian\,\micro s. Over
\ddTriples{} triples of consecutive labels on a track,
\ddInterpBelowThresh\,\% of middle box centers fall within a hundredth of a
pixel of their neighbors' linear interpolant. This rules out exact local linear
interpolation as a general description of the released trajectories without
identifying the underlying annotation process. DSEC-Det ships more than one annotation
version~\cite{beyondduality2026}, the supplement names the one measured here.

Median box-center image speed is
\labelSpeedMedian\,px/s, with \labelSpeedPninetynine\,px/s at the ninety-ninth
percentile.

\subsection{Mains-Frequency Signature and Per-Pixel Phase Test}
\label{sec:line}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\figasset{figs/fig7_ceiling_vs_day.pdf}{0.95\columnwidth}
\caption{Top: 350\,\micro s slices of the ceiling-exposure sequence
\texttt{zurich\_city\_09\_a} and of the daytime control at the instants when the
ceiling sequence's own event rate reaches its peak and trough inside its densest
published exposure window. Bottom: that rate in 350\,\micro s bins, each
sequence normalized to its own mean, the ceiling rate moves by a factor of
\ceilVarNight{} between its extremes, the daytime rate by \ceilVarDay{}.}
\label{fig:flickerreal}
\end{figure}

Swiss mains is \mainsHz\,Hz, and rectified lighting can produce \flickerLineHz\,Hz
intensity modulation. The observed event-rate spectrum contains the
corresponding harmonic series because event cameras respond to log-intensity
change.
(Fig.~\ref{fig:flickerreal}). Sweeping \harmGridLo--\harmGridHi\,Hz on each whole recording, with no
band fixed in advance and each frequency divided by the median of its own
neighborhood, returns that series in every ceiling sequence: the ceiling median
is \harmOne{} at \flickerLineHz\,Hz, \harmTwo{} at \harmSecondHz\,Hz and
\harmThree{} at \harmThirdHz\,Hz, and the second harmonic is the strongest line
in \harmSecondStrongest{} of the \dsecCeilingSeqs{}, never falling below
\harmTwoMin{}. At the odd
multiples of \mainsHz\,Hz there is nothing: \harmFifty{}, \harmOneFifty{} and
\harmTwoFifty{} at \mainsHz{}, \harmOddOneHz{} and \harmOddTwoHz\,Hz. This harmonic pattern is
consistent with rectified 50-Hz illumination and is absent from the daytime control. The
daytime sequence carries the fundamental at \harmDayOne{} and the second harmonic
at \harmDayTwo{}, against \harmTwoMin{} for the weakest ceiling sequence.

Per pixel, the Rayleigh statistic $Z=R^{2}/N$ is $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ under
independent uniform phases. The off-frequency and daytime controls empirically
calibrate this nominal null, while the ceiling sequence has median
$Z=\flickerZmedian{}$ at \flickerLineHz\,Hz and
\flickerFracLockedPct\,\% of live pixels reach $p<10^{-3}$.

\subsection{All six ceiling sequences, per labeled box}

The same statistic taken per labeled box, over the events inside that box
during that frame's own exposure window, extends to every ceiling sequence,
the supplement tabulates all \dsecCeilingSeqs{} of them over \sixBoxes{}
boxes. Across the six ceiling sequences, \sixLockedLoPct{}--\sixLockedHiPct\% of boxes satisfy
the locked criterion defined in Supplement Table~2.


\subsection{Within-box temporal dispersion under that signature}
\label{sec:cost}

That signature limits attribution of within-exposure event timing to object timing.
Within-box dispersion is \sigmaEvtNight\,\micro s against a null of
\sigmaEvtNullNight\,\micro s, with an excess of \sigmaEvtExcessNight\,\micro s.
A frame-level permutation preserving pooled temporal distributions and box counts
gives a null of \permNull\,\micro s. The excess remains after the clean-pixel
control, while scene and illumination components remain unresolved.

\section{Limitations}

Results use the released artifacts, local occlusion sensitivity, nominal-time
greedy matching, the reported specification, and local constant velocity.
Correlated annotation-error bias and the full recurrent centroid remain
unidentified. Gen1 and DSEC are separate case studies. DSEC dispersion is not
object-specific.

\section{Conclusion}

A nominal benchmark timestamp is not a temporal specification. The predictor
exhibits distinct input-side sensitivity and a regression-based temporal
coefficient on nominal-time-matched detections, while the DSEC case study shows
that illumination structure limits the attribution of within-exposure event
timing to object motion.
